passages.t: ‘Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt’
passages.happening:
“So Israel set out with all that he had, and when he came to Beersheba, he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac” (verse 1).

That night God speaks to him in a vision. “Jacob, Jacob!” “Here I am” (verse 2).

“I am God,” He said, “the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make you into a great nation there” (verse 3). “I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back. And Joseph's own hands will close your eyes” (verse 4).

Jacob's sons carry him in the wagons Pharaoh sent. They take their children, their wives, their livestock and everything they own. “Jacob and all his offspring went to Egypt” (verses 5-7).
passages.hearers:
Beersheba was at the southern edge of Canaan, on the road to Egypt. It was a holy place in this family's memory. Abraham planted a tree there and called on the LORD (21:33). God appeared to Isaac there and said, ‘Do not be afraid, for I am with you’ (26:24). Jacob stops at the last place of worship before he leaves the land.

Why might Jacob be afraid? Egypt had gone badly for Abraham (chapter 12). God once told Isaac not to go down to Egypt at all (26:2). And God had told Abraham that his descendants would be ‘strangers in a land that is not their own’ and be enslaved (15:13). Leaving the promised land was a serious step.

So God speaks. “Jacob, Jacob!” The doubled name is how God calls someone at a turning point. He did it to Abraham on the mountain (22:11).

God makes three promises. He will make Jacob a great nation in Egypt. He will go down with him. And he will bring him back. Then a fourth, tender one: Joseph will close his eyes. Closing the eyes of the dead was done by someone close. It means Jacob will die with his son beside him.

This is the last time God speaks to Jacob in Genesis.
passages.later:
God called Moses the same way at the burning bush: “Moses, Moses!” “Here I am” (Exodus 3:4). And God kept his word. In Egypt “the Israelites were fruitful and increased rapidly” (Exodus 1:7).

Isaiah gives the same promise to God's people in a later trouble: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you” (Isaiah 43:2). Matthew tells how the child Jesus too was taken down to Egypt, and he applies Hosea's words to him: “Out of Egypt I called My Son” (Matthew 2:15).
passages.asks: God did not promise Jacob that Egypt would be easy. He promised to go down with him. Ask what hard place you are being asked to go into. Then ask whether ‘I will go with you’ is enough for you, even without knowing how it will turn out.

passages.happening:
“Now these are the names of the sons of Israel (Jacob and his descendants) who went to Egypt” (verse 8).

The list goes mother by mother. First Leah's sons and their sons, with Dinah, thirty-three in all (verses 8-15). Then Zilpah's, sixteen (verses 16-18). Then Rachel's, with Joseph's two sons born in Egypt, fourteen (verses 19-22). Then Bilhah's, seven (verses 23-25).

“All those belonging to Jacob who came to Egypt” numbered sixty-six, not counting the wives of Jacob's sons (verse 26). “And with the two sons who had been born to Joseph in Egypt, the members of Jacob's family who went to Egypt were seventy in all” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Lists like this are easy to skip. But for the first hearers, these were their own family names. Many of them became the names of Israel's clans.

The list is built by Jacob's four mothers of sons. Leah's line is the largest. Each servant's line is about half her mistress's: Zilpah's sixteen to Leah's thirty-three, Bilhah's seven to Rachel's fourteen.

Only two women are named among the descendants: Dinah, Jacob's daughter, and Serah, Asher's daughter. The wives are not counted at all (verse 26). That was how such lists were usually made.

Notice two small notes. One of Simeon's sons is ‘the son of a Canaanite woman’ (verse 10). The family was already marrying into the land. And Judah's line names Perez and Hezron (verse 12), from the story of Tamar.

The numbers take care. Sixty-six leaves out Jacob himself, Joseph and Joseph's two sons. Add those four, and you reach seventy. The thirty-three of Leah's line seems to count Jacob too. Seventy is also a number of fullness. By the usual count, the Hebrew list of nations in Genesis 10 holds seventy names. Some see the small family of promise as a little copy of the whole world it was meant to bless.
passages.later:
Moses later reminds Israel how small they began: “Your fathers went down to Egypt, seventy in all, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars in the sky” (Deuteronomy 10:22). Exodus begins with the same count: “The descendants of Jacob numbered seventy in all” (Exodus 1:5).

Matthew's family line of Jesus runs through these names: “Perez the father of Hezron” (Matthew 1:3).
passages.hard:
Genesis says seventy. Stephen, in Acts, says “seventy-five in all” (Acts 7:14). Which is right?

The two numbers come from two forms of the Old Testament. The Hebrew text of Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 says seventy. The Septuagint, the old Greek translation of the Old Testament made before the time of Jesus, says seventy-five in Genesis 46:27. It adds more descendants of Joseph's sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. Stephen was speaking in a Greek-speaking setting, and his number follows that Greek form of the text.

So the difference is not between Stephen and Genesis so much as between two ways of counting the same family. Some readers have suggested other ways to reach seventy-five, such as adding some of the wives. Either way, neither number is a head count of everyone who travelled. Wives and servants are left out. These lists aim to show a whole family, not to give a census.

The same kind of care helps with Benjamin's ten sons (verse 21). Numbers 26:40 names two of them, Ard and Naaman, as Benjamin's grandsons. Many readers think this list is arranged by clans, and may include some born later in Egypt.
passages.asks: Seventy names, and God would make them a nation. Ask whether your own small beginnings seem too small for God to use. Then ask whose names are on the list of your family of faith, and whether you thank God for them.

passages.happening:
Jacob sends Judah ahead to Joseph to get directions to Goshen (verse 28).

“Joseph prepared his chariot and went there to meet his father Israel. Joseph presented himself to him, embraced him, and wept profusely” (verse 29).

“Then Israel said to Joseph, ‘Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!’” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Judah goes ahead. He is now the brother Jacob trusts to lead.

Goshen was a region of Egypt, usually placed in the eastern Nile delta, nearest to Canaan. Its exact borders are not known.

The reunion is told in very few words. Joseph rides out in his chariot, a sign of his high rank. Then he ‘presented himself’: in Hebrew, he let himself be seen. He falls on his father's neck and weeps, and keeps weeping.

Last time Jacob saw his son, Joseph was a boy of seventeen in a fine robe, setting out to check on his brothers (37:14). Twenty-two years have gone by. Jacob mourned him the whole time.

Jacob's words are not gloomy. ‘Finally I can die’ means: I am at peace now. I have seen what I needed to see. He will in fact live another seventeen years (47:28).
passages.later: Old Simeon in the temple spoke in the same way when he held the baby Jesus: “Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace. For my eyes have seen Your salvation” (Luke 2:29-30).
passages.asks: Jacob said he could die in peace once he had seen his son's face. Ask whose face you are longing to see, in this life or the next. Then ask what peace would mean for you, and where you are looking for it.

passages.happening:
Joseph tells his family how to meet Pharaoh. He will go and tell Pharaoh that they have come: “The men are shepherds; they raise livestock” (verse 32).

When Pharaoh asks their work, they are to say, “Your servants have raised livestock ever since our youth” (verse 34).

“Then you will be allowed to settle in the land of Goshen, since all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Joseph knows the court. He coaches his family to tell the plain truth: they are herders. That truth will earn them land of their own, a little apart.

Why would shepherds be ‘detestable’ to Egyptians? It is honestly hard to say. Egypt was a land of settled farmers, and Egyptians kept flocks and herds of their own. No clear Egyptian text is known that says shepherds as such were hated. Much later, Herodotus wrote that Egyptians despised swineherds, but that is a different matter. Many readers think the dislike was of foreign herders who moved with their flocks across the border. Others suggest other reasons. The narrator states it as a fact of his world without explaining it.

What is known is that herders from the east did come into the delta in hard times. A painting in a tomb at Beni Hasan, from the 1800s BC, shows a group of people from the east arriving in Egypt with their donkeys and goods. A much later Egyptian letter, Papyrus Anastasi VI, from the late 1200s BC, reports that border officials let herders from Edom pass into the delta to keep themselves and their flocks alive.

The separation helped Israel too. Living apart in Goshen kept the family from being swallowed up by Egypt. They stayed a distinct people.
passages.later: Shepherding runs all through Israel's story. Moses was keeping sheep when God called him (Exodus 3:1). David was the shepherd boy who became king (1 Samuel 16:11). A psalm says, “The LORD is my shepherd” (Psalm 23:1). And Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).
passages.asks: Joseph told his family to tell the plain truth about their humble work, even though some looked down on it. Ask whether you hide what you do, or where you come from, to win approval. Then ask what it would cost to be honest about it.
